problem: Costmap-based navigation treats all free space as traversable and relies on purely geometric perception, so it ignores behavioral conventions (keep right, pass on left, slow near cars) and misclassifies soft obstacles like curtains. Learning-based language navigation needs large datasets and generalizes poorly, and prior hybrid methods (BehAV, INF) either lack traversability handling or directional/behavioral preferences.
motivation: Robots in human environments must produce socially compliant trajectories, not just collision-free ones, yet most deployed stacks are costmap-based planners. Injecting LLM-parsed language constraints into costmaps can add behavioral awareness while keeping the planner's efficiency, modularity and reliability.
key_idea: Parse natural-language behavioral instructions with an LLM into (object, direction, velocity, traversability) tuples, ground them with camera-LiDAR open-vocabulary segmentation, and encode them as multi-layer costmaps consumed by an unmodified A*/TEB planner.
insight: Semantic constraints are best expressed as cost fields in the existing planner's representation rather than as LLM-generated actions, which retains planner speed and safety. The alpha ablation (Fig. on interpolation) shows a tradeoff: alpha<1 gives conservative paths with weak side compliance, while alpha>1 yields stricter compliance. Baselines like BehAV and InstructNav completely fail on traversable-obstacle tasks (0% SR), which shows that semantic override of LiDAR geometry is a key component.
method: Behavioral instruction parsing: Qwen-VL-Max turns offline (global) and online (situational) instructions into tuples C={(O_i,d_i,v_i,t_i)} with direction {left,right,middle}, velocity {slow,normal,fast}, traversability {traversable,non-traversable}.

Semantic object modeling: GSAM2 produces open-vocabulary masks; LiDAR points projected into the mask are denoised with DBSCAN, aggregated over a sliding window and reduced to a BEV axis-aligned bounding box.

Geometric and semantic traversability layers: C_geo marks obstacle cells from height-filtered non-ground points (255 vs 100); C_sem overrides LiDAR by marking boxes traversable/non-traversable, inferred from mean geometric cost vs a threshold when unspecified.

Directional constraint layer: three costs (c1,c2,c3) across the box's lateral axis set by left/right/middle rules, with piecewise non-linear interpolation (exponent alpha=3), and the box is inflated for non-traversable objects.
Velocity constraint layer: box cells are assigned cmin/mid/cmax for slow/normal/fast; the cost at the robot's cell is mapped to a translational speed limit sent to the local planner.

Costmap fusion and planning: C_spat (geo+sem+dir) is fed to A* global planning and TEB local planning without planner modification, while C_kin regulates speed. Costmap resolution is 0.05 m over 10x10 m.

setting.backbone: Qwen-VL-Max (frozen, instruction parsing) + GSAM2 (frozen, segmentation) + A* / TEB planners
setting.action_space: velocity commands from TEB local planner over A* global path (continuous, with speed limit from kinematic costmap)
setting.privileged: none (goal point manually set; human teleoperated reference path used only for the FD metric)

numbers_note: Custom simulation tasks, no standard benchmark or official split (split 'test' is a placeholder). Number of trials is not stated (SR values in multiples of 10% suggest 10). Alpha ablation, speed and real-world results are qualitative figures only.
results: NORM-Nav reaches 90% SR in region following, region avoidance and combined tasks and 80% in traversable-obstacle tasks, with lower Fréchet distance to human paths. It beats BehAV (60/60/0/30% SR) and InstructNav (50/40/0/20%), and INF (70% SR, 52.14% SPL on traversable obstacles). Real-world demos show side-specific compliance and passing through curtains.
limitations: Small-scale evaluation (apparently about 10 trials per task, one simulator environment), with real-world results only qualitative demonstrations
Depends on the accuracy of GSAM2 grounding and LLM parsing, and uses axis-aligned BEV boxes that approximate objects coarsely
INF was only evaluated on the traversable-obstacle task, so comparisons are incomplete; no analysis of latency or LLM failure cases
